method: PubMed E-utilities searches; every cited source's abstract was fetched in this session. Effect sizes are as reported in the abstract. Findings are paraphrased.

demands.finding: Basketball is intermittent and high-intensity: across a 40-minute game players cover roughly 5-6 km of live-time movement and spend much of it above lactate threshold and above 85% of maximal heart rate. Vigorous activity drops in the fourth quarter. Men and women at the same level face similar demands. (Mostly adult and elite samples.)

In elite under-19 players, sprinting took about 5% of live time and jumping about 2%; mean heart rate was about 171 beats/min and blood lactate averaged about 5.5 mmol/L, higher at half time than at full time. So both the aerobic base and repeat-sprint/anaerobic capacity matter.

Accelerations, decelerations, jumps and multidirectional shuffling make up the mechanical load. In elite junior female players (about 17 years old), acceleration-to-deceleration ratios rose with high-intensity efforts in close fourth quarters; the authors recommend eccentric strength and specific conditioning, especially before tournament-style congested schedules.

In female basketball, accelerometer 'player load' rises with competitive level and is higher in games than practice. Small-sided games (3v3) produced more load and distance than 5v5, so coaches can use court size and player numbers to progress conditioning in practice.

Key qualities, based on these profiles: repeated sprint and change-of-direction ability, vertical jump and landing capacity, eccentric braking strength for decelerations, and an aerobic base that supports recovery between bursts.

injuries.finding: US high school surveillance (2005-2014): boys' time-loss injury rate was 1.55 per 1000 athlete-exposures (AEs) and girls' 1.82; game rates were about 2.4x (boys) and 3.0x (girls) practice rates. The commonest injuries were ligament sprains, muscle/tendon strains and concussions, mostly to the ankle, knee and head/face. Contact with another player and non-contact mechanisms caused most injuries.

Meta-analysis across basketball studies: ACL injury rate was 0.20 per 1000 AEs in females vs 0.07 in males (about 3.3x higher in females), and about 8x higher in games than practice. Ankle sprains were the more common injury overall (about 0.8-0.9 per 1000 AEs), slightly more common in males, and also higher in games.
In youth (11-18) soccer and basketball players in Canada, basketball carried about 1.8x the ankle-sprain risk of soccer, and a previous ankle sprain doubled the risk of another.

In US high school sports, season- or career-ending injuries were about 1.6x more common in girls' than boys' basketball; the knee (most often the ACL) was the commonest site of these disqualifying injuries.

Jumper's knee (patellar tendinopathy) was present in about 32% of Norwegian elite male basketball players, and basketball was among the sports with the highest prevalence in a Dutch survey of non-elite athletes.
Among sex-comparable high school sports (including basketball and soccer), girls had about 2.2x the concussion rate of boys (2013-2018 surveillance).

differences: Spend more live time sprinting and in high-intensity shuffling, and less time standing/walking, than forwards and centers; they show higher heart rates and blood lactate.
Among male professionals they cover the most distance and perform the most accelerations and decelerations.
Perform more high-speed and high-intensity running than other positions in male professional samples.

Less live time in high-intensity activity than guards (about 14.7% vs 17.1% in elite U19); more rebounding and contact-heavy work. Some studies report higher heart rates in centers, so findings are mixed.
In elite junior females, centers showed more variable output across quarters, which the authors suggest needs position-specific conditioning.

riskReduction.finding: A coach-delivered 10-minute neuromuscular warm-up (SHRed Injuries Basketball) lowered ankle and knee injuries in youth players aged 11-18, and it worked as well unsupervised as supervised.
riskReduction.dose: 10 minutes as the practice warm-up, every session, through a season
riskReduction.effect: 36% lower ankle and knee injury rate (IRR 0.64, 95% CI 0.51-0.79)

riskReduction.finding: A coach-led 20-minute neuromuscular warm-up in Chicago public high schools reduced non-contact lower-limb injuries in girls' soccer and basketball.
riskReduction.dose: 20 minutes before practice; used in about 80% of practices
riskReduction.effect: Non-contact lower-limb injuries IRR 0.33; non-contact ankle sprains 0.38; non-contact knee sprains 0.30; non-contact ACL 0.20

riskReduction.finding: A multicomponent warm-up in regional-level adult basketball players cut ankle sprains and non-contact lower-limb injuries.
riskReduction.dose: Whole season, as the team warm-up
riskReduction.effect: Ankle sprain IRR 0.26 (95% CI 0.05-0.98); trend toward fewer knee injuries

riskReduction.finding: Pooled youth soccer and basketball data: exposure to a neuromuscular warm-up was protective against ankle sprains.
Plyometric/landing training before the season reduced serious knee injuries in high school female basketball, soccer and volleyball players to about the male rate.
riskReduction.effect: Knee injury 0.43 vs 0.12 per 1000 AEs (untrained vs trained girls); no non-contact knee injuries in trained girls

warmup.finding: Neuromuscular training warm-ups are recommended as the minimum standard of practice in youth basketball by the SHRed trial authors; coach delivery without study staff gave the same benefit.
Warm-ups that combine running, strength, plyometrics, balance and agility have the strongest evidence in high school girls' basketball.

adolescent.finding: High school game injury rates are 2-3x practice rates, so match play is when knee and ankle exposure peaks.
Interventions aimed at middle and high school-aged athletes reduce ACL injuries more than those aimed at college or professional athletes (OR 0.38 vs 0.65).

demands.finding: Volleyball is a short-burst, jump-dominated sport. A 2026 systematic review of match play found setters perform the most jumps overall, while middle blockers and outside/opposite hitters perform the most high (>50 cm) jumps. Female players jump more often but lower than males and report higher internal load.
In NCAA Division I women, jump load was higher in practice than in matches, and about 75% of landings were two-footed. Practice volume, not just matches, is where most jump-landing load comes from.
Key qualities: vertical jump and reach, repeated jump-landing tolerance, reactive agility for defense, and shoulder power and endurance for serving and attacking.

injuries.finding: US high school girls' volleyball (2005-2014) time-loss injury rate was 1.11 per 1000 AEs, higher in games than practice (IRR 1.23) and higher in smaller schools. Ankle sprains were common; liberos had a notably high share of concussions.
Common volleyball injuries across levels are ankle sprains, patellar tendinopathy, finger and thumb sprains, overuse shoulder problems and concussions.
In youth (12-18) volleyball, mostly female, the ankle, then wrist/hand/fingers, then the knee were the most injured sites.
In Dutch club players, ankle sprains were 41% of all injuries, and 75% of players who sprained an ankle had sprained it before. Overuse injuries were mainly back and shoulder.

Mechanism: in world-class volleyball, most ankle injuries happened while blocking and landing on an opponent's foot under the net, or a back-row attacker landing on a front-row teammate; the ankle rolled into rapid inversion without much plantarflexion.
Jumper's knee prevalence was about 45% in Norwegian elite male volleyball players and 14% in Dutch non-elite players, the highest of the sports surveyed; men had about twice the prevalence of women.

In elite male university and professional players, average weekly prevalence of knee, low back and shoulder problems was 31%, 21% and 19%; most players reported some complaint during the season and many played with pain.
Landing from a jump caused 57-82% of ACL injuries in overhead sports such as volleyball (video and case analyses).

differences: Highest total jump volume in match play.
Shorter and with lower jump output than middle blockers in some samples; greater shoulder extension range than other roles in one sensor study.
Most high jumps (>50 cm); middle blockers are tallest with highest block and spike reach and best squat/countermovement jumps.
Blocking at the net is the main ankle-sprain situation.
Defensive specialists with lower jump output but fast agility; high perceived exertion in matches.
High share of concussions in US high school and college surveillance (dives and collisions).

riskReduction.finding: A proprioceptive balance-board program in volleyball players reduced ankle sprains, but only in players with a previous sprain; it raised overuse knee injuries in players with a previous knee injury.
riskReduction.effect: Risk difference 0.4 ankle sprains per 1000 playing hours

riskReduction.finding: Across volleyball prevention studies, programs aimed at the ankle reduced ankle injuries.
riskReduction.effect: Ankle injuries fell from about 0.9 to 0.5 per 1000 player hours

riskReduction.finding: A shoulder-focused warm-up added twice a week reduced total injuries and injury severity in recreational volleyball players, with a significant shoulder-injury reduction in men.
exercises: rotator cuff and scapular exercises in the warm-up
riskReduction.dose: Start of each training session, twice per week
riskReduction.effect: Significant drop in total injuries; shoulder injuries lower (significant in males)

riskReduction.finding: For overhead athletes, three modifiable shoulder risk factors guide prevention: loss of internal rotation (GIRD), weak external rotators, and scapular dyskinesis.
riskReduction.effect: Narrative and systematic review evidence; range of motion, cuff weakness and training load are the key modifiable factors

riskReduction.finding: Neuromuscular training reduced ankle sprains in female court-sport athletes including volleyball; comprehensive programs (strength, balance, plyometrics, agility) gave the clearest effect.
riskReduction.effect: 2 of 7 studies significant, others trending; benefit greatest for non-contact sprains

warmup.finding: A volleyball-specific shoulder warm-up is feasible and protective in recreational players, though compliance needs work.
Neuromuscular warm-ups in high school girls including volleyball players reduced serious knee injuries.

adolescent.finding: Youth volleyball injury data are thin (5 studies, mostly girls), with ankle, hand/finger and knee as the main sites.
Prospective screening of jump height, ankle dorsiflexion, balance and landing mechanics did not predict jumper's knee in elite men, so managing jump load is a more practical lever than screening.

demands.finding: Soccer is a mixed aerobic-anaerobic sport. Professional female players cover about 9.5 km per match, with roughly 580 m of high-speed running plus many sprints, accelerations and decelerations.
High-intensity actions in elite soccer have increased over time and include not only straight sprints but curved sprints, changes of direction and jumps, which differ by position and tactical role.

Key qualities: aerobic capacity, repeated sprint ability, acceleration and deceleration strength, change of direction, and eccentric hamstring and adductor strength (the two muscle groups most often strained).

injuries.finding: US high school soccer (2005-2014): boys' time-loss injury rate 1.83 and girls' 2.33 per 1000 AEs; game rates were 3.6x (boys) and 4.9x (girls) practice rates. Most injuries were to the lower extremity (sprains and strains). Concussion made up more than a fifth of boys' and about 25% of girls' high school game injuries.

Youth (19 and under) meta-analysis: about 5.7 injuries per 1000 hours in boys and 6.8 in girls; match rates (about 14-15 per 1000 h) far exceed training (about 2.6-2.8). Boys most often had muscle/tendon injuries, girls joint/ligament injuries; injury rates rose with age in boys.
In young soccer players, the ankle and thigh are most injured in boys and the ankle and knee in girls; maturity status and age affect risk.

US high school ACL injury rate was 13.2 per 100,000 AEs in girls vs 4.4 in boys (about 3x); competition rates were 15x (girls) and 9x (boys) practice rates; a smaller share of girls' ACL tears involved player contact (30% vs 49%).
Across team ball sports, 55% of ACL injuries are non-contact (63% in females), and non-contact ACL incidence is nearly 3x higher in females (0.14 vs 0.05 per 1000 h).
In girls' soccer and basketball, concussions are more common than in boys; soccer concussions mostly come from player contact rather than purposeful heading.

differences: Performance depends on sprint, jump, agility and mobility rather than long-distance aerobic capacity.
Injured less often than field players overall but with position-typical injuries (hands, shoulders, head).
More than one-third of competition injuries to US high school girls' goalkeepers were concussions; concussion was also common in college male goalkeepers.
Carry the running load (high-speed running, sprints, accelerations/decelerations), varying by tactical role; the main injury burden is lower-limb sprains and strains.

riskReduction.finding: FIFA 11+ reduced overall soccer injuries by 39% in recreational/subelite players; the older FIFA 11 showed no effect.
riskReduction.dose: About 20 minutes as the warm-up, at least 2x per week

riskReduction.finding: A comprehensive warm-up (the 11+ precursor) in Norwegian girls aged 13-17 reduced overall, overuse and severe injuries.
FIFA 11+ Kids in boys aged 7-13 cut injuries by more than half.
exercises: age-adapted balance, strength, falling technique and agility
riskReduction.dose: At least twice a week as warm-up for 6 months

riskReduction.finding: In NCAA men, FIFA 11+ lowered knee and ACL injuries.
riskReduction.dose: 15-20 minutes before every training and game for a season
riskReduction.effect: Knee injury RR 0.42; about a 4-fold reduction in ACL injuries

riskReduction.finding: Network meta-analysis: FIFA 11+ was the most effective program for ACL risk in soccer overall; in females only Knäkontroll showed a significant effect.
riskReduction.effect: Ranked first overall for FIFA 11+; Knäkontroll best for females (low certainty)

riskReduction.finding: Adding the Nordic hamstring exercise to prevention programs halves hamstring injuries across sports and in soccer specifically.
riskReduction.dose: Within warm-up/training programs (doses varied across trials)

riskReduction.finding: A single-exercise Copenhagen adduction program cut groin problems in semiprofessional men.
riskReduction.dose: 3x/week for 6-8 weeks of preseason, then 1x/week in season
riskReduction.effect: Groin problem prevalence 13.5% vs 21.3%; odds 41% lower

riskReduction.finding: In female athletes, ACL programs work best with landing stabilization and lower-body strength (Nordic hamstrings, lunges, calf raises) and trained implementers.
riskReduction.effect: ACL risk from 1 in 54 to 1 in 111 (OR 0.51)

warmup.finding: Pooled FIFA 11+ trials show a protective effect in males of all ages; evidence in females is less certain in one 2025 meta-analysis.
The 11+ Kids version is effective and practical for children's teams.

adolescent.finding: Faster growth in height and leg length was linked to more injury in elite male youth players, with peak risk around 92-95% of predicted adult height; large week-to-week jumps in training exposure added risk.

A targeted program for academy players in the growth spurt (modified load, balance/coordination/landing drills and individual strength work) cut injury incidence in the highest-risk group (rate ratio 0.14).
Youth heading frequency is low and rises with age; girls head less but sustain higher impact magnitudes, and stronger necks may help.

demands.finding: Meta-analysis of match play: average rally lasts about 5.5 s (men) to 6.4 s (women) with about 4 strokes; effective playing time is only about 19-20% of match time. International men run about 9.6 m per point and 2.3 km per best-of-five match.

Work-to-rest ratios are roughly 1:3 to 1:5; competitive players need speed, agility and power on top of a good aerobic base (VO2max typically above 50 mL/kg/min in men). Fatigue reduces hitting accuracy.

Mechanical load is dominated by frequent accelerations, decelerations and multidirectional changes of direction, with heart-rate peaks during rallies. Lower- and upper-limb strength-power, stretch-shortening ability and trunk control support performance and robustness.
The serve is the most demanding stroke and makes up 45-60% of strokes; elite players hit about 40 serves per set, which gives a 'unit dose' for planning serve volume.
Serving games cause higher oxygen uptake, heart rate and perceived exertion than returning, and longer rallies raise heart rate.

injuries.finding: High-performance juniors: about 2.1-3.5 injuries per 1000 hours and 46-54% seasonal prevalence. Lower-limb injuries are about half; lumbar spine (12-39%) and shoulder overuse follow.
Most tennis upper-limb injuries are overuse; risk factors include high exposure, scapular dyskinesis, fatigue, shoulder mechanics, skill level and technique.

Lumbar MRI abnormalities are very common even in symptom-free elite juniors: 85% abnormal in one study, with pars (L5) stress lesions in about a quarter to a third of players and early facet joint changes.
Rotator cuff injuries in younger players are usually partial-thickness overuse tears from repeated serving; shoulder range-of-motion deficits and scapular dyskinesis can appear right after a match.

positions.position: Not applicable (individual sport); serving vs returning roles within a match
differences: Serving games are physiologically harder than return games.
Men serve more per set than women; professionals serve more per set than juniors.

riskReduction.finding: Load control: sudden spikes in workload (acute:chronic ratio of 1.3 or more in juniors) were the strongest extrinsic injury predictor; four-week ramp-up strategies reduced incidence.
Kinetic-chain conditioning (core stability plus eccentric rotator cuff training) reduced overuse injuries and kept shoulder mobility.
Grip-size personalisation halved lateral elbow pain in one prevention cluster.

In elite juniors, previous injury, fewer years of experience (upper-limb), playing more than 6 hours/week and previous back injury (low back) were the risk factors with moderate evidence. No randomized prevention trials in juniors were found.
Shoulder prevention in overhead athletes centres on internal-rotation range, external-rotator strength and scapular control.

warmup.finding: No tennis-specific warm-up trial was found in this search; the evidence base is load management and kinetic-chain conditioning (see riskReduction).

adolescent.finding: Expert review guidance for juniors: avoid single-sport specialization before about 12, train no more hours per week than age in years (maximum 16), cap organized tennis around 12 h/week, keep at least 2 h/week of injury-prevention training, no more than 2 tournaments a month, and be wary of more than 40 matches a year. (Low-to-moderate quality evidence.)
Pars stress lesions are common in elite adolescents and linked to facet joint angle, so persistent low back pain in a junior player warrants assessment.

demands.finding: Golf is low aerobic intensity but each swing is a high-speed rotational effort. In competitive youth golfers, peak power explained about 80% of the variation in clubhead speed and isometric peak force about 70-74% of carry distance; maturity status also strongly predicted clubhead speed.
Strength and conditioning programs (strength, plyometrics, stretching, core) improved clubhead speed, ball speed and distance by about 4-6% on average where effects were significant.
Key qualities: lower-body and rotational power, isometric strength, hip and trunk mobility, and trunk muscular endurance.

injuries.finding: Lifetime injury prevalence is about 57% in amateurs and 74% in professionals; professionals have about 3x more hand/wrist and low back injuries. Soft-tissue injuries dominate. Playing more than 3-4 rounds a week raised amateur risk. (Mostly adult samples, mean age 47.)
Pooled injury incidence is about 2.5 per 1000 rounds (18 holes), higher in professionals than amateurs.
Low back pain is the most common golf complaint. Older age, higher body mass and previous back pain are associated; swing characteristics were not clearly linked in pooled data.
Trunk muscle activation, hip strength and mobility, and pelvis/trunk rotation patterns are the biomechanical factors most associated with low back pain in golfers.
In US emergency departments, 10-19 year olds made up about 11% of golf-related lower-limb injuries, and golf carts caused about 40%, so many youth golf injuries are not from swinging.

differences: Professional vs amateur differs mainly by volume: professionals have more wrist and back injuries.

riskReduction.finding: A pre-game golfers' low back pain prevention program in adolescents improved lead-hip external rotation strength compared with sham, without hurting golf performance (injury outcomes not yet reported).
riskReduction.effect: Greater lead-hip ER strength vs sham; hip ROM and trunk endurance improved in both groups

riskReduction.finding: Strength and conditioning for golf (strength, plyometrics, core) improves swing outputs; the same qualities (hip strength, trunk control) are those linked to back pain.
riskReduction.effect: About 4-6% gains in clubhead/ball speed and distance

riskReduction.finding: A randomized trial of a 6-exercise, 10-minute golf injury prevention warm-up (GRIPP) is under way; no golf injury-prevention RCT result was available at protocol publication.

warmup.finding: Many golfers do not warm up or do very short warm-ups. Dynamic warm-ups and those with resistance exercise improved performance, static stretching did not and may hurt it; links between warm-up habits and injury were inconclusive.

adolescent.finding: A 2026 scoping review found adolescent golf injury data are sparse and often mixed with adults; no study linked training volume to injury risk in juniors.
In youth golfers, maturity status explains much of clubhead speed, so comparisons between juniors of the same age should account for growth.

demands.finding: Baseball is power-dominant with long rests: short sprints, throws and swings. In 1157 professional players, lower-body power rose into the mid-20s while 10-yard sprint and agility stayed stable across ages and positions.
Throwing velocity drives arm load: in high school pitchers (13-18), throwing harder in games and an in-season rise in velocity relative to preseason were injury risk factors.
Key qualities: rotational and lower-body power, sprint acceleration, and shoulder range of motion and cuff/scapular strength to tolerate repeated throwing.

injuries.finding: US high school baseball (2005-2014): 0.98 time-loss injuries per 1000 AEs, about 2.3x higher in games than practice. Upper-extremity injuries were most common, and many happened while fielding or pitching; being hit by pitched or batted balls is a recurring mechanism.

Half of 9-14 year-old pitchers had elbow or shoulder pain in one season; more pitches per game and per season raised pain rates, and curveballs and sliders were associated with more shoulder and elbow pain.
Over 10 years, 5% of youth pitchers had a serious throwing injury (surgery or retirement); pitching more than 100 innings in a calendar year raised risk 3.5x.
In Japanese junior high players, 28% developed shoulder and/or elbow pain over a year; throwing 300 or more full-effort balls a week and 10 or more games a month were elbow-pain risk factors.

Prospective-study review: in youth, history of elbow pain, being a pitcher or catcher, ages 9-11, more than 100 innings a year and over 16 training hours a week were elbow-injury risk factors; shoulder range and strength deficits predicted arm injury in high school and professional players.
Hamstring strains were about 1.7x more common in college baseball/softball men than women; most strains overall were non-contact and preseason rates were about twice in-season rates.

differences: Highest throwing-arm load; pitchers report worse arm health scores and about 2x the odds of an upper-limb overuse injury compared with non-pitchers in high school.
Velocity, intensity, pitch counts and innings drive risk.
Catchers share elevated elbow and shoulder pain risk with pitchers in youth surveys.
High school pitchers who also played catcher had 2.9x the shoulder/elbow injury risk (15% vs 5%).
Lower arm load; injuries more often from fielding, base running and being struck by the ball.

riskReduction.finding: A warm-up of stretching, dynamic mobility and balance exercises cut shoulder and elbow throwing injuries in 9-11 year olds and tended to raise ball speed.
In high school pitchers, nightly external-rotation strength training was at least as good as sleeper stretching for preventing arm injuries (and had a lower observed rate).

Screening shoulder rotation: insufficient external rotation (less than 5 degrees more than the other arm) roughly doubled shoulder-injury risk in professional pitchers; total rotation or flexion deficits of 5 degrees or more raised elbow-injury risk about 2.6-2.8x.

Workload rules: pitch-count limits work better than inning limits for controlling volume; parents who knew and followed Pitch Smart guidelines had children with fewer injuries, and showcase participation predicted injury.
riskReduction.dose: Per game, per week and per year limits
riskReduction.effect: Inning-limited and longer-mound leagues threw more pitches; guideline-aware families had fewer injuries

warmup.finding: A structured mobility-and-balance warm-up reduced throwing injuries in youth players (Japanese RCT).

adolescent.finding: Highly specialized high school players had 3.8x the odds of an upper-limb overuse injury; playing more than 8 months a year doubled the odds.

Proximal humeral and medial elbow growth-plate stress injuries occur in young baseball players (shoulder changes in up to about 37% in cross-sectional imaging); most heal with timely rest, but some cause growth disturbance when diagnosis is late.
Pitch count guidelines were introduced in 1996 and revised in 2006; adherence by coaches, parents and players is often poor.

demands.finding: Fastpitch softball shares baseball's short-burst power profile (sprinting, swinging, throwing). Bat swing velocity at a fixed bat load related to in-game batting statistics in NCAA Division I players.

The windmill pitch produces shoulder and elbow loads similar to baseball pitching, with very high eccentric biceps activity (about double that of an overhand throw), especially at the 9 o'clock phase.
Key qualities: hip, core and lower-body strength for the pitching and hitting kinetic chain, and shoulder/biceps endurance for pitchers.

injuries.finding: US high school softball (2005-2014): 1.16 time-loss injuries per 1000 AEs, about 2x higher in games. Ankle sprains and concussions were the commonest injuries, many while fielding or running bases.
Softball was the one girls' high school sport where fracture was the most common season- or career-ending diagnosis.
Windmill pitchers mainly get overuse injuries (anterior shoulder and biceps), though apparently at lower volume than baseball pitchers.

differences: High school pitchers' pain and fatigue rose over a single game and over the season, with falls in shoulder flexion, supraspinatus and external rotation strength as games pitched increased.
One study found more than 85 pitches per game raised season injury risk; no US or Canadian pitch-count rules existed as of 2023.
Most injuries come from fielding, base running (ankle sprains) and being struck by the ball.

riskReduction.finding: Surveillance authors recommend strength training and ankle-sprain prevention programs plus protection from batted and pitched balls.
For windmill pitchers, prevention and rehabilitation should focus on mechanics, core, hip and lower-body strength, and recognising fatigue.
Multicomponent exercise programs reduce ankle injuries in high school athletes across sports (applicable to softball's ankle-sprain burden).
riskReduction.dose: High adherence; frequency and duration matter

warmup.finding: No softball-specific warm-up trial was found; general high school multicomponent programs reduce ankle injuries.

adolescent.finding: Fatigue in high school pitchers builds across a season with no pitch limits in place, so coaches should track pitches and games and watch for pain.

crossCutting.finding: In high-level team sports, females had about 2.2x the ACL rate of males while males had more upper-limb, hip/groin, thigh and foot injuries; ankle sprains and concussions did not differ significantly.
In contact sports (which include basketball and soccer), females had 3x the ACL incidence of males.
Across eight meta-analyses, ACL prevention programs halve ACL injuries in all athletes and cut non-contact ACL injuries in females by two-thirds.
More neuromuscular training is better: longer and more frequent sessions gave larger ACL reductions in females (high volume OR 0.32 vs low 0.66).
For female team athletes, compliance of 75% or more mattered most; sessions over 15 minutes, 2-3 times a week, with agility and running mechanics, reduced knee injuries (ACL risk halved).
Exercise-based prevention reduced ankle injuries by 26% in high school athletes; best programs were multicomponent, emphasised strength and agility, and had high adherence and coach education.
ACL injury situations by sport: change of direction (26-70% in team sports) and landing (57-82% in overhead sports such as volleyball) dominate.
Highly specialized youth athletes had about 1.8x the overuse injury risk of low-specialization athletes.
Specialization is usually defined as choosing a main sport, quitting others, and training more than 8 months a year; sports medicine bodies recommend multisport participation.
In elite youth athletes, injury burden rises with maturity and growth-related injuries peak in the growth spurt; faster growth in height and leg length means more injury.

Growth-plate (periphyseal) stress injuries appear across repetitive youth sports including baseball, tennis, volleyball and soccer; about 13% of reported cases caused growth disturbance, usually with delayed diagnosis or no rest.
In US high school sex-comparable sports, girls' concussion rate was 2.2x boys'.
